task.name: hardening: enforce per-test timeouts in gate runs
task.story_text:
CONVENTIONS.md states that every test must complete in under five seconds and
that no test may perform blocking I/O without a timeout. Nothing enforces it. The
rule is advisory prose, so a test that violates it is discovered only when it
consumes an entire gate run.

When that happens the gate's verdict carries no attribution. The suite is killed as
a whole, so the run ends without a complete verdict and without naming the test
that consumed the budget. Whatever the log happens to show before the kill — some
assertion failures, the termination line — the one thing it cannot supply is which
test was responsible, and whether it was slow or genuinely blocked.

## Why

Re-evidenced on 2026-08-29. A sprint on #2681 cycled through repeated DEV
iterations without ever establishing whether the branch's tests passed: a newly
added production wait caused pre-existing, previously-compliant coordinator tests
to block, and the suite was terminated past ten minutes with no summary. The
absence of a named culprit then produced competing reconstructions of the failure,
none of which the artifacts could settle quickly.

The bound cannot be enforced by asking developers to honour it. The tests that
blocked here were not written in violation of the rule — they were compliant when
written, and a change elsewhere in the tree made them slow. No authoring-time
discipline reaches that case; only an enforced budget does.

## Acceptance criteria

- The test configuration checked into the repository declares a per-test time bound
  matching the documented five-second rule, and whatever the runner needs in order
  to enforce it is a declared development dependency rather than an assumption
  about the environment.
- The bound is declared once, in configuration, so that every invocation of the
  suite inherits it without a flag being passed — the project gate, the developer
  check, and a bare runner invocation in a terminal alike. An invocation nobody
  anticipated inherits the bound rather than escaping it.
- A test that blocks past the bound is named in the run's output together with a
  stack trace locating where it was stuck, so the run's failure is attributable
  rather than anonymous. A deterministic test demonstrates this using its own short
  bound, so the demonstration does not add the default bound's duration to every
  run.
- The baseline suite remains green under enforcement without skips, broad
  exclusions, or widening the shared bound.
- A per-test override may shorten the bound — for example, for a deterministic test
  that proves the enforcement works. No test in the default suite may raise it
  above the shared five-second bound; validation that legitimately needs longer
  belongs outside the default gate.

## Example

Today, a coordinator test that blocks on a real polling path ends the run like this
— no test name, no stack trace, no exit status:

```
........................................F...............   [ 91%]
make: *** [dev-check] Terminated: 15
```

Afterwards the same test should be named as having exceeded the bound, with a stack
trace showing where it was stuck, so the failure is attributable to it rather than
to the run as a whole.

## Observed on the two failed attempts (measured 2026-08-30)

Both dev iterations implemented the bound and both deadlocked the suite. Direct
measurements on an idle machine:

- Base branch `make gate`: **92s** wall clock, 10,296 passed, 0 failed.
- With enforcement configured as `timeout = 5` / `timeout_method = "signal"` under
  `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`, alongside the pre-existing
  `addopts = "-n auto --dist worksteal"`: the run reaches ~99%, stops, and never
  finishes — still running past **600s**, versus 92s green on base.
- At that point all ten xdist workers are alive at **0.0% CPU**. Sampling one shows
  its main thread parked acquiring a lock, and its execnet receiver thread blocked
  reading from the master:

```
main-thread
  ... method_vectorcall_VARARGS_KEYWORDS
        lock_PyThread_acquire_lock
          acquire_timed
            PyThread_acquire_lock_timed      <-- parked here indefinitely

receiver thread
  _io__Buffered_read -> _bufferedreader_raw_read -> _io_FileIO_readinto
    -> _Py_read -> read
```

Zero CPU across every worker distinguishes this from a slow suite: nothing is
executing, and nothing will wake up. The gate reports only
`TIMEOUT after 360s: make gate`, so neither iteration was ever shown this.

Related hazard already recorded in CONVENTIONS.md: forked xdist workers that inherit
a held lock deadlock. This is evidence of what happens, not a prescription for which
enforcement mechanism to use.

events.criterion: The baseline suite remains green under enforcement without skips, broad exclusions, or widening the shared bound.
events.undefined_case: The criterion assumes the pre-existing suite is already compliant with the five-second rule, but it is not. Measured on this branch, several pre-existing tests take 1.8-3.3s serially and cross 5s under the gate's own `-n auto --dist worksteal` parallelism: tests/test_issue_body_producer_conformance.py::TestSeamRegistry (the lru_cached `_all_seams()` AST scan of src/theforge, ~2.1s serial, re-paid per worker because the cache is per-process), tests/test_protected_base_publication_poc.py (1.8-3.1s serial, real git subprocesses via memory_publication.prune_merged_staged_memory), tests/test_sprint_run_artifact_publish_timing.py (1.9-3.3s serial), tests/test_sprint_parallel.py and tests/test_sprint_terminal_lifecycle.py. Enforcement itself is not the cost: the same file runs 3.76s without enforcement and 3.83s with it serially, so there is no overhead left in my implementation to remove. The criterion does not say what to do when the baseline itself violates the bound being enforced, and the three permitted remedies it names (no skips, no broad exclusions, no widening) plus the instruction not to edit those test files leave no action that satisfies everything.
events.assumption: I will make the over-budget tests faster in place, editing those existing test files as the minimum needed to bring them under the bound - primarily by making the `_all_seams()` scan cheap enough to re-pay per worker (or shared across workers), and by reducing the real-subprocess work in the sprint/publication tests. I will not widen the bound, add skips, or add exclusions. If a test cannot be brought under 5s without changing what it actually verifies, I will report it as still failing rather than weaken its coverage.
options_considered: Speed up the offending tests in place (edit those existing test files), keeping the 5s bound and full coverage - satisfies every AC literally but requires touching files the feedback said not to edit.

Land enforcement and move the demonstrably over-budget tests behind an existing opt-in marker with their own make target, outside the default gate, as the AC's own 'validation that legitimately needs longer belongs outside the default gate' clause allows for.

Land enforcement and reduce the cascade rather than the tests: the 92s to 196s slowdown comes from timeout-kills triggering xdist worker restarts that re-collect 10k tests; capping worker count or restarts in the gate command would shrink contention, but that changes the Makefile and does not fix tests that are over budget on their own.
Treat the near-bound cluster as a separate follow-up story, landing enforcement now and accepting a known-red gate until those tests are fixed.

resolutions.answer: There is no specification gap. The baseline-green criterion requires bringing existing default-gate tests exposed as over budget under the five-second bound while preserving their coverage. Those tests are directly related to this story, so the generic prohibition on modifying unrelated existing tests does not apply. Do not skip, exclude, re-mark, or widen the bound. If a specific test cannot meet the bound without losing coverage, stop and report that case.

handoff.summary: Enforced CONVENTIONS.md's five-second per-test rule as configuration rather than prose. pyproject.toml declares timeout = 5 and timeout_method = "thread" under [tool.pytest.ini_options] with pytest-timeout as a declared dev dependency, so the gate, make dev-check, and a bare pytest all inherit the bound with no flag. The method must be thread: the signal method deadlocks every xdist worker at 0% CPU under the existing -n auto --dist worksteal addopts. Because the thread method ends a timed-out test with os._exit(1), which in an xdist worker kills the process before pytest-timeout's stack dump reaches the controller, tests/timeout_enforcement.py wraps pytest_timeout.timeout_timer to write the culprit's nodeid plus thread stacks into a controller-created temp directory on the way to exit, and re-emits them under a 'per-test timeout stack dumps' heading at terminal summary. The same module rejects timeout marks that widen the bound, disable it (0/negative), or change enforcement (method=, timeout_method=, func_only=True), reporting the violation as a named test failure at setup rather than crashing an xdist worker at collection. tests/conftest.py re-exports the hooks so the real suite loads them; the module is also loadable standalone via -p timeout_enforcement, which is how the demonstration child project gets the identical support. An earlier revision of the dump channel armed faulthandler.dump_traceback_later around every test; that reproduced the spec's own 99% stall symptom on make dev-check, so it was replaced with the zero-extra-thread wrapper, and a test now guards against reintroducing it.

acceptance_criteria.notes: validate_timeout_mark accepts shorter numeric overrides (positional and keyword) and rejects timeout(6), timeout(timeout=6), timeout(0), negative values, method=/timeout_method= (keyword and positional), func_only=True, and non-numeric or bool values without crashing collection. Marks are read via iter_markers so module-level pytestmark and parametrized marks are covered. Violations are stashed at collection and raised as a named failure at setup, deliberately not as a collection-time exception, because under xdist collection runs in the workers where raising would crash the worker instead of naming the test.

story_deviations: Plan Step 2 offered fd-level stderr capture or faulthandler as the stack-preservation mechanism; the plan reviewer had already measured fd redirection as non-functional. I implemented faulthandler first per the reviewer's suggestion, measured it deadlocking make dev-check at 99% (the spec's own signal-method symptom), and replaced it with a wrapper around pytest_timeout.timeout_timer. This is strictly better: it runs on pytest-timeout's existing timer thread, so it adds no threads and does no per-test work, and only the process that actually timed out ever writes a file — which also removes the reviewer's concern about non-culprit workers emitting unattributed dumps, without needing per-test arm/cancel.

Plan Step 3 said to reject overrides via a collection hook. Validation does happen at collection, but the rejection surfaces as a named failure in pytest_runtest_setup rather than an exception during collection, because under xdist collection runs in the workers and raising there produces a worker crash instead of an attributable failure.

Implementation lives in tests/timeout_enforcement.py with hooks re-exported from tests/conftest.py, rather than wholly in tests/conftest.py as Steps 2 and 3 described. This is what lets the Step 4 child project load the identical support with -p timeout_enforcement instead of duplicating it, which the plan reviewer flagged as required.

Not addressed here: fixing it means either speeding up or re-marking existing test files unrelated to this story, and the ACs forbid widening the bound or adding skips. Needs the authoritative gate result to know whether it is a problem on the gate machine at all.

In a serial (non-xdist) run the thread method still calls os._exit(1) in the controller process, so terminal summary never runs and the dump directory is left in the system temp dir. Harmless and self-limiting (one small directory, only on a run-ending timeout), and serial runs already print pytest-timeout's own dump to the real terminal, so attribution is not lost there.

handoff.summary: Addressed the gate failure by fixing what my change exposed rather than by weakening the bound. The dominant cause was tests/test_issue_body_producer_conformance.py: its `_all_seams()` repository scan cost ~1.9s per process and, being lru_cached per process, was re-paid by every xdist worker, so its parametrized cases crossed five seconds under `-n auto` and accounted for 17 of the gate's 25 failures. I made the scan exact-but-cheap in two ways: skip the AST parse for files that provably cannot hold a seam (both seam kinds require the literal token `issue`, which drops 182 of 341 files, with the same reasoning behind a `#!` guard on the embedded-hook walk), and walk each function once and index the result instead of re-walking the whole function per candidate list, which was O(functions x tree) and accounted for 2.7M ast.walk steps. Both were verified equivalent rather than merely faster: `_python_seams` returns identical output on all 341 files and `_all_seams()` returns an identical mapping; the scan drops 1.90s to 0.63s and the file's slowest test under xdist drops 4.1s to 1.3s with all 57 tests passing and no coverage removed. The gate's 18th failure was my own attribution demonstration, whose xdist child spawned three processes and spiked to 13.3s of startup contention on a saturated machine; it now drives a genuine pytest timeout in a single child process (0.76-1.29s worst case under the same load) and is backed by two new in-process tests of the dump write and the controller-side re-emit that cannot flake. Supporting that, a controller handed THEFORGE_TIMEOUT_DUMP_DIR now uses it and leaves it in place, which also closes a real gap I had previously only noted: in a serial run the timeout kills the controller itself, so cleanup never runs and a self-made temporary directory stranded the one artifact worth having. CONVENTIONS.md was corrected, since it still described the per-test faulthandler timer from an earlier revision that was measured deadlocking the suite at 99%. Local `make dev-check` is now 70.7s against the gate's failing 196s.

acceptance_criteria.notes: Anchored on tests that cannot flake: test_the_culprit_and_its_stack_survive_the_worker_exit covers the dump write that runs on pytest-timeout's timer thread immediately before os._exit(1) plus the controller re-emit; test_a_worker_that_never_timed_out_leaves_no_dump proves only the timing-out process writes anything; test_a_real_timeout_names_the_blocked_test_and_where_it_was_stuck drives a genuine pytest timeout in a child process with its own 0.25s bound and reads back the recovered dump. The mechanism has repeatedly proven itself in practice: every diagnosis in this story started from a gate dump naming a culprit with its stack, including this cycle's memory_publication:389 lead.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: The baseline suite remains green under enforcement without skips, broad exclusions, or widening the shared bound.
acceptance_criteria.notes: No skips, exclusions, re-marking, or widening anywhere. Gate has gone 25 to 13 to 7 to 4 failures, run time 196s to 76s. The four remaining are one family, all under the bound serially: test_protected_base_parallel_merge_pr_poc 3.06s, test_assignment_history_learning_end_to_end 2.53s, test_a_reachable_refusal_is_prevented_by_the_publication_seam 1.93s, test_a_non_landing_workflow_is_unaffected 1.62s. They need 1.6x to 3x inflation to cross five seconds, which is what -n auto produces on a saturated machine. Across three cycles I have ruled out every candidate cause by measurement: zero seconds slept; the lease sweep is 8% with an effective prune (average one surviving candidate); no pathological repeated command; audit rendering already halved; memory publication is 39% of the worst test but flat across many small git calls; the fixtures are lean (113 of 137 spawns in the smallest failing test are production code); and the repeated commands are mutable state that cannot be cached without staleness bugs. These tests are thin wrappers around a real sprint over real git, and the git work is the coverage — this is the case the operator's gap answer asked me to stop and report.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A per-test override may shorten the bound — for example, for a deterministic test that proves the enforcement works. No test in the default suite may raise it above the shared five-second bound; validation that legitimately needs longer belongs outside the default gate.
acceptance_criteria.notes: validate_timeout_mark accepts shorter numeric overrides (positional and keyword) and rejects timeout(6), timeout(timeout=6), timeout(0), negative values, method=/timeout_method= (keyword and positional), func_only=True, and non-numeric or bool values without crashing collection. Marks are read via iter_markers so module-level pytestmark and parametrized marks are covered. Violations are stashed at collection and raised as a named failure at setup rather than as a collection-time exception, because under xdist collection runs in the workers where raising would crash the worker instead of naming the test.

story_deviations: Four production files were changed across this story, each because a hard-coded timing or repeated-work choice was what put tests over the bound, and each preserving existing behaviour and defaults. process_group.py: three grace defaults now take None and resolve through a `_grace` helper at call time, so KILL_GRACE_SECONDS is one knob rather than four copies. sprint/runner.py: the scheduling loop's 2.0 literal is now the named constant PLAN_GATE_TICK_SECONDS with the same value. cli/shared.py: the run audit is rendered once per content state instead of once per copy, which also removes real duplicated work from every production run completion.

Existing test files were modified (test_issue_body_producer_conformance.py, test_no_test_double_detection_guard.py, test_process_group.py, test_sandbox_group_kill.py, test_sprint_terminal_lifecycle.py, test_sprint_parallel.py). The standing rules would normally protect these, but the operator's resolution of gap 1 states the tests exposed as over budget are directly related to this story and must be brought under the bound with coverage preserved. No assertion was removed or weakened; the changes shorten durations the tests do not assert, and equivalence was verified where a scan was optimised.

Two deliberate timeouts that tests waited out were shortened because the duration was not what they assert: the lifecycle teardown trigger from 2s to 0.5s, and the sandboxed group-kill agent timeout from 5s to 3s.
deferred_items: Four tests remain over the bound under gate parallelism while being under it serially, all driving a full sprint through the real runner over real git: test_protected_base_parallel_merge_pr_poc (3.06s), test_assignment_history_learning_end_to_end (2.53s), test_a_reachable_refusal_is_prevented_by_the_publication_seam (1.93s), test_a_non_landing_workflow_is_unaffected (1.62s). Three things would resolve this and all are operator decisions rather than dev ones: reduce gate parallelism (-n auto oversubscribes, and the plan explicitly told me not to change Makefile commands); restructure this family into narrower tests that do not each drive a full sprint, as a separate story; or accept the bound and treat the family as needing that follow-up. The enforcement itself is working correctly — it is what identified every one of these.

Optimisations considered and rejected on evidence across cycles: libyaml's CDumper for the audit writer (produces different bytes, unsafe for a persisted format); caching the per-release process-table sweep (measured at 8% with an effective prune, and it is a containment safety net); collapsing _branch_sync_delta's two rev-list calls (about 0.1s, but inverting left/right would silently swap ahead/behind in operator-facing warnings); batching the 35 cat-file existence checks into one --batch-check (about 0.3s and 31 spawns, but needs stdin plumbing into a shell-string helper in the publication path); caching repeated sprint git commands (they re-read mutable state, so caching would introduce staleness bugs).

Tests that skip locally but run on the gate are a standing blind spot for duration work: 38 skip locally against 29 on the gate, and the sandboxed group-kill test was over budget by construction for that reason alone. Measuring durations in an environment where the platform sandbox is reachable would close it.

The run audit reaches ~81KB and is fully re-serialised on each completion. Rendering once per state removed the duplicate copies, but the underlying full-document rewrite per completion remains a scaling cost that append-only writes would address.

Step 2 says to accept numeric timeout marks <= 5. pytest-timeout treats zero or negative values as disabled because its runtest hooks arm a timer only when settings.timeout > 0; therefore @pytest.mark.timeout(0) would pass collection and remove the shared bound. The plan's own Risk 2 mitigation asserts that the thread method yields 'culprit nodeid and stack trace in output'. plan_structured.approach: Use pytest-timeout as the declared runner dependency, keep the five-second default in `pyproject.toml`, and enforce with `timeout_method = "thread"` because the measured `signal` method deadlocks under the existing xdist `-n auto --dist worksteal` configuration. Since pytest-timeout's thread handler exits xdist workers before their stderr stack dump reaches the controller, add repository pytest support that preserves worker timeout stack dumps and re-emits them from the controlling pytest process. Keep collection-time validation that timeout marks may only shorten the bound and may not disable or alter the enforcement mode. Prove attribution with a child pytest project that mirrors the xdist/worksteal execution path using a short deterministic timeout.

steps.description: Declare the shared per-test timeout and compatible enforcement mechanism in pytest configuration.
steps.details: Keep `pytest-timeout` in `[project.optional-dependencies].dev`. Under `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`, set `timeout = 5` and change/add `timeout_method = "thread"`; leave the existing `addopts = "-n auto --dist worksteal"` in place so gate, dev-check, and bare pytest invocations all inherit the same bound from configuration.

steps.description: Preserve and surface timeout stack dumps from xdist workers.
steps.details: Add small pytest support for xdist runs so thread-mode timeout dumps are not lost when a worker exits via `os._exit(1)`. The controller should create a per-run temporary timeout-dump directory and expose it to workers through inherited environment or xdist worker input; each worker should capture fd-level stderr or otherwise write pytest-timeout/faulthandler timeout output to a per-worker file before tests run; the controller should re-emit any timeout dump files during terminal summary or session finish so the main run output includes the culprit nodeid and the stuck stack frame even when xdist reports the worker as crashed. Keep this scoped to test-run diagnostics and avoid changing Makefile commands or adding timeout CLI flags.

steps.description: Enforce that collected tests may only shorten the shared timeout.
steps.details: Add a collection hook that inspects every collected item's `timeout` marks, including marks applied through module `pytestmark` or parametrization. Read numeric timeout values from `mark.args[0]` and `mark.kwargs.get("timeout")`, coercing to float while handling `None`, invalid, or non-numeric values without crashing collection. Reject any numeric override unless `0 < timeout <= 5`, because zero or negative disables pytest-timeout. Reject mark options that alter enforcement rather than only shortening duration, including `method`, `timeout_method`, or `func_only=True`; in particular reject signal-method and func-only overrides. Accept absent marks and valid shorter numeric overrides. Do not add skips, marker exclusions, or a path allowlist.

steps.description: Add focused tests for configured inheritance, declared dependency, no per-invocation timeout flags, override validation, and attributable timeout output under xdist.
steps.details: Test `pyproject.toml` declares `timeout = 5`, `timeout_method = "thread"`, and a `pytest-timeout` dev dependency. Assert repository runner commands do not pass `--timeout`. Add tests exercising the collection hook with allowed `@pytest.mark.timeout(1)` and rejected overrides for `timeout(6)`, `timeout(timeout=6)`, `timeout(0)`, negative values, `method="signal"`, and `func_only=True`; include an invalid/non-numeric mark case to prove the hook handles it gracefully. Keep the child project minimal and measure the parent test so it remains under the repository's own five-second per-test bound; if the worker-crash path cannot fit, change the stack-preservation mechanism so the xdist demonstration completes within the bound rather than raising or disabling the parent timeout.
